q.q: Which statement about the Internet and the World Wide Web is correct?
o: The Web is one service that runs over the Internet
The Web and the Internet are two names for the same thing
The Internet is one service that runs over the Web
Email and video calls are both part of the Web
q.why: The Internet is the infrastructure; the Web is a service that uses it, alongside email, file transfer and others.

q.q: What is the Internet?
o: A collection of linked hypertext documents accessed using HTTP
A global network of interconnected networks using the TCP/IP protocols
A single very large network owned and run jointly by a group of the biggest ISPs
A set of web servers that store every website in the world
q.why: The Internet is the hardware plus agreed protocols; linked hypertext documents are the Web.

q.q: Why was TCP/IP devised?
o: So that web pages could be written in HTML and displayed in any browser
So that domain names could be translated into numeric IP addresses
So that incompatible networks such as ARPANET, NPL and CYCLADES could be joined
So that data sent across all the different networks could be encrypted with TLS
q.why: TCP/IP allowed internetworking: joining networks that could not otherwise talk to each other.

q.q: Who proposed the World Wide Web, and where?
o: Tim Berners-Lee at the NPL in England in 1969
The IETF in the USA, as part of ARPANET
The W3C in 1994, as a successor to ARPANET
Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989
q.why: Berners-Lee proposed the Web at CERN in 1989 and CERN released it free in 1993; he founded the W3C later, in 1994.

q.q: What is a website?
o: A single hypertext document written in HTML
A set of related web pages sharing a common domain name
The client program that displays web pages
A computer that stores the pages and delivers them to browsers
q.why: A web page is one document; a website is a related set of pages on the same domain.

q.q: Which answer would gain full marks as a definition of a web server?
o: A computer that stores web pages and sends them to browsers on request using HTTP
A computer that is connected permanently to the Internet by an ISP
A program that requests web pages and displays them for the user
A company that rents out storage space on its servers so that a site is available online
q.why: A full definition says what it is and what it does; the other options describe a host, a browser or a vague computer.

q.q: What service does a web hosting company provide?
o: A connection to the Internet for homes and businesses
Software that interprets the HTML, CSS and scripts of each page you visit
Space on permanently connected servers to store and serve a site
The root servers of the Domain Name System
q.why: Hosting packages typically include storage, traffic allowance, email, databases, backups and statistics.

q.q: What is an Internet service provider's point of presence?
o: The router in a customer's home that shares the connection
The web server on which a customer's site is hosted
The DNS resolver that translates domain names for customers
Its access point for an area, to which customers connect
q.why: An ISP connects customers to its point of presence; the home router then shares the one connection.

q.q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?
q.why: IPv4 uses 32 bits, written as four 8-bit octets; IPv6 uses 128.

q.q: Convert the IPv4 address 10101100 00010000 11111110 00000001 to dotted decimal.
Which of these is a valid IPv4 address?
q.why: Each of the four octets must be 0–255; 256 is out of range and colons and hex are used in IPv6.

q.q: How is an IPv6 address written?
o: Eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons
Four groups of denary numbers from 0 to 255 separated by full stops
Eight groups of denary numbers from 0 to 255 separated by colons
Four groups of eight binary digits separated by hyphens
q.why: IPv6 uses 128 bits in eight hex groups, e.g. 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329.

q.q: Why was IPv6 introduced?
o: IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out as phones and smart devices connected
IPv4 addresses could not be translated into domain names by DNS
IPv4 addresses were too long for people to remember easily
IPv4 could not carry encrypted HTTPS traffic safely between devices on different networks
q.why: 128 bits gives about 3.4 × 10^38 addresses, solving the shortage.

q.q: In www.qub.ac.uk, what is the top-level domain?
o: www
qub
ac.uk
uk
q.why: The TLD is the right-most label; ac.uk is a sub-domain of uk.

q.q: In www.belfastzoo.co.uk, which is the organisation's registered domain?
o: co.uk
belfastzoo.co.uk
www.belfastzoo.co.uk
belfastzoo
q.why: Reading right to left: uk is the TLD, co.uk the sub-domain for companies, belfastzoo.co.uk the organisation's domain and www names its web server.

q.q: What does the Domain Name System do?
o: Translates IP addresses into MAC addresses
Encrypts the traffic between browser and server
Translates domain names into IP addresses
Stores web pages and delivers them to browsers
q.why: DNS converts a name into an IP address, not the other way round.

q.q: When your device looks up a domain name, which server does it usually ask first?
o: A root server, which holds every domain's records
A DNS resolver, usually run by the ISP
The web server named in the domain
The authoritative server for the top-level domain
q.why: The resolver queries down the hierarchy from root to TLD to authoritative servers and returns the address.

q.q: Why are DNS answers cached for a set time?
o: To speed up later look-ups of the same name
To encrypt the results of each look-up
To stop sites ever changing their IP address
To store a backup copy of every web page
q.why: Caching avoids repeating the full look-up each time.

q.q: In https://www.translink.co.uk/timetables/metro.html?route=9a, which part is the query string?
o: https://
www.translink.co.uk
?route=9a
/timetables/metro.html
q.why: The query string passes data to a server-side script; the path identifies the folder and file.

q.q: Which three parts does every URL contain?
o: Protocol, IP address and port number
Domain name, query string and status code
Protocol, path and session ID
Protocol, domain name and path
q.why: A URL says how to fetch the resource, which server holds it, and where on that server it is; the query string is optional.

q.q: A server returns the status code 404. What does this mean?
o: The request succeeded
There was an internal server error
The requested resource was not found
The user is not logged in
q.why: 200 is OK, 404 is Not Found and 500 is Internal Server Error.

q.q: What does HTTPS add to HTTP?
o: Faster downloads by compressing every page and image
Proof that the website's owner is honest and that its products are trustworthy
A different domain name for each secure page on a site
Encryption of data in transit and authentication of the server
q.why: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: data is encrypted and the server proves its identity with a certificate.

q.q: Why is plain HTTP unsuitable for sending a password?
o: Everything is sent as readable text, so anyone intercepting it can read it
HTTP cannot carry form data, so passwords must be sent by email
HTTP is stateless, so the server forgets the password immediately
HTTP compresses the password with a lossy method, which changes some of its characters
q.why: Without TLS the traffic is unencrypted.

q.q: Which protocol would a developer use to upload a site's pages to a web host?
o: HTTP
FTP (or SFTP)
DNS
SMTP
q.why: FTP transfers files of any type in either direction, with authentication.

q.q: What is anonymous FTP used for?
o: Uploading pages securely to a host
Resolving domain names into IP addresses for the public
Encrypting email attachments
Letting the public download files without logging in
q.why: No credentials are needed, so it is used only for public downloads.

q.q: Why are SFTP or FTPS now preferred to classic FTP?
o: Classic FTP sends passwords unencrypted
Classic FTP can only download files
Classic FTP cannot transfer images
Classic FTP needs no username or password
q.why: Secure versions encrypt the credentials and data.

q.q: What does it mean to say HTTP is stateless?
o: Each request is encrypted so that no one except the server can read the state of the connection
Each request is independent and the server keeps no memory of earlier requests
The server stores every request so it can be replayed later
Pages cannot change once they have been sent to the browser
q.why: Every transaction stands alone.

q.q: What are the two main advantages of HTTP being stateless?
o: It is secure against interception and remembers each user automatically
It keeps users logged in and remembers what is in their basket
It is simple to implement and efficient with server and network resources
It encrypts every request and caches every page on the server
q.why: Nothing needs to be remembered between requests, so the protocol is simple and uses minimal resources.

q.q: What is a cookie?
o: A small program downloaded with a page and run by the browser to check each form field as it is typed
A record of a visit stored on the server and identified by a random number
A small piece of text stored by the browser and sent back with later requests to that site
A copy of a web page kept on a proxy server to reduce network traffic
q.why: The browser returns the cookie with every request, so the server can recognise the visitor.

q.q: What is the difference between a session cookie and a persistent cookie?
o: A session cookie is deleted when the browser closes; a persistent one lasts until its expiry date
A session cookie is stored on the server; a persistent one is stored in the browser
A session cookie is set by advertisers; a persistent one is set by the site itself
A session cookie is encrypted with TLS; a persistent one is always stored and sent as plain readable text
q.why: Lifetime is the difference; third-party cookies are set by advertisers.

q.q: Why are server-side sessions more secure than storing basket and login data in a cookie?
o: Sessions are sent using FTP, which encrypts every request
The data stays on the server, and the device holds only a random session ID
Cookies cannot be deleted by the user once the browser has stored them on the device
Sessions are faster because they are cached by a proxy
q.why: Sensitive information never sits on the user's device where it could be read or altered.

q.q: Why do third-party tracking cookies raise privacy concerns?
o: They are stored on the server, so users cannot see or delete them at all
They contain the user's password in plain text for every site visited
They last only until the browser closes, so no record of the user's consent can ever be kept
They are set by advertisers embedded in many sites and can follow a user across the Web
q.why: Tracking across many sites builds a profile of the user's browsing.

q.q: Which UK rules require sites to obtain consent before storing non-essential cookies?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
PECR together with the UK GDPR
The Disability Discrimination Act 1995
q.why: The Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations and the UK GDPR govern cookies and consent.

q.q: What is the main benefit of a proxy cache in a school?
o: Content requested by many users is stored once locally, reducing traffic and waiting time
It encrypts pupils' passwords before they are sent to any website
It replaces the DNS so that every domain name is resolved inside the school instead of by the ISP
It blocks all cookies so that pupils cannot be tracked by advertisers
q.why: Shared caching saves bandwidth for everyone.

q.q: Why might a live-scores page tell caches not to store it?
o: So the page can be encrypted with TLS
So users do not see stale, out-of-date content
So the server can remember each visitor and their basket
So the page loads faster from the cache
q.why: Rapidly changing content should be fetched fresh.

q.q: Which component of a search engine follows links from page to page to discover content?
o: Index
Query engine
PageRank
Web crawler
q.why: The crawler (spider) starts from seed pages and follows every link it finds.

q.q: Where does a web crawler begin?
o: From a list of seed pages
From the root DNS servers
From the most recent search queries
From the page with the highest PageRank
q.why: It collects links on the seed pages, then visits each linked page in turn.

q.q: How can a site owner ask crawlers to avoid certain pages?
o: By removing the page's metadata
With a robots.txt file
By using HTTPS on those pages
By setting a persistent cookie
q.why: robots.txt tells crawlers which pages not to visit.

q.q: How is a search index organised?
o: As a list of URLs in the order the crawler found them, searched from start to finish
As a copy of each page's HTML, scanned in full whenever a user makes a query
As a ranked list of the most popular sites, ignoring the words on each page
Like a dictionary, so each word can be looked up instantly to find every page containing it
q.why: The index is built in advance for instant look-up.

q.q: What does PageRank mainly measure?
o: How quickly a page loads on mobile devices
How many times the search terms appear in the text and title of the page
How many pages link to a page, weighted by the linking pages' own rank
How recently the page was last updated
q.why: Links act like weighted votes.

q.q: Why might a brand-new web page not appear in search results?
o: Search engines search the live Web, which takes days to complete
New pages have no metadata until a search engine adds it
Pages without HTTPS are never added to any search index
Results come from the index, and the page has not yet been crawled
q.why: Results are not a live search of the Web; they come from the index.

q.q: What is metadata on a web page?
o: Data about the page, such as its title and description
The visible paragraphs and images on the page
The IP address of the web server that is hosting the page
The list of links that point to the page
q.why: Metadata describes the page but is not part of its visible content.

q.q: Which job is done by the query engine?
o: Following links from seed pages to discover new pages
Storing the words and metadata of every page visited
Looking up the search terms in the index and ranking the matching pages
Asking site owners for permission to visit their pages using robots.txt
q.why: The crawler discovers, the index stores and the query engine matches and ranks.

q.q: Which body agrees the standards for HTML and CSS?
o: ITU
W3C
IETF
ISP
q.why: The W3C is responsible for web content languages and guidelines, including WCAG.

q.q: Which is the ITU's main area of standardisation?
o: The languages used to write web content, such as HTML and CSS
The core Internet protocols, such as TCP, IP, DNS and HTTP
The rules that search engines must use to rank pages fairly in their results
How data is carried and formatted, e.g. over cable, radio and satellite links
q.why: ITU-T covers transmission, codecs, certificate format and spectrum.

q.q: Which body develops core Internet protocols such as TCP, IP, DNS and TLS, publishing them as RFCs?
o: W3C
ITU
IETF
CERN
q.why: The IETF is an open, largely volunteer community of engineers.

q.q: Which standards body defined the X.509 format used for digital certificates?
o: W3C
ITU
IETF
WHATWG
q.why: The notes list X.509 certificates under the ITU's data-format work.

q.q: Who founded the W3C, and when?
o: Tim Berners-Lee in 1994
The United Nations in 1865
Tim Berners-Lee in 1989
CERN in 1993
q.why: He proposed the Web in 1989 and founded the W3C in 1994.

q.q: What is the main benefit of web standards for users?
o: Pages load and work correctly even without any Internet connection
All websites become free to use
Pages work consistently in any standards-compliant browser on any device
Users no longer need passwords to log in
q.why: Interoperability is the key benefit.

q.q: How do standards encourage competition and choice?
o: Only the companies on the standards committee are allowed to build compatible devices
Standards set the price of browsers and routers so that all suppliers charge the same
Each manufacturer writes its own standard, so users can choose between incompatible ones
Any company can build a compatible browser, router or phone, so users are not locked in
q.why: Shared specifications let many suppliers make interoperable products.

q.q: Which statement about the standards bodies is correct?
o: The W3C specifies web content; the ITU deals with how data is formatted and transmitted
The ITU specifies HTML; the W3C allocates radio frequencies
The W3C lays the undersea cables; the ITU publishes the accessibility guidelines for web pages
The IETF publishes WCAG; the W3C defines TCP and IP
q.why: The ITU is not responsible for HTML, and the W3C does not lay cables or allocate spectrum.

q.q: What is a dynamic web page?
o: A page stored as a fixed file that every visitor sees in the same form
A page generated when it is requested, often from data in a database
A page that contains animations or video that move on screen
A page that cannot be stored in a browser or proxy cache
q.why: Dynamic pages are built on demand, so they can be personalised and kept current by changing the data.

q.q: Where does a client-side script run?
o: In the user's browser
On the web server
On the DNS server
In the database
q.why: Client-side code, usually JavaScript, is downloaded with the page and run by the browser.

q.q: Why is server-side code considered more secure than client-side code?
o: It is encrypted by the browser before it runs on the device
It is written in HTML, which cannot contain any errors
It runs faster, so attackers have less time to intercept it
It never leaves the server, so users cannot see or alter it
q.why: Client-side code is downloaded, so it can be read, switched off or altered.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of server-side scripting?
o: The code is downloaded with the page, so users are able to read it, switch it off and change it
Every action needs a round trip to the server, and busy sites need powerful servers
It cannot query or update a database held on the web server
Browsers may run it slightly differently, so results vary
q.why: The other options are client-side drawbacks or untrue.

q.q: A bus company's site shows the timetable for route 9A when it is chosen. What happens after the web server passes the request to a server-side script?
o: The browser runs JavaScript to download the whole database to the device
The server sends the database file to the browser to build the page
The script queries the database and builds an HTML page around the results
The browser queries the database directly using the query string
q.why: The script runs a query such as SELECT, builds HTML and the server returns it; the browser is unaware it was built on demand.

q.q: Which job is best done by a client-side script?
o: Checking a password against the stored record
Checking a form field as the user types
Taking a card payment
Updating stock levels in the database
q.why: Client-side scripts give instant responses; passwords, payments and database updates belong on the server.

q.q: What is SQL injection?
o: A server-side script inserting new records into a database once the input has passed validation
A browser downloading JavaScript with a page and running it automatically
An attacker typing SQL into a form field hoping it will be executed by the database
A database being restored from a backup after it has been corrupted
q.why: Malicious input is treated as SQL code.

q.q: Which defends against SQL injection?
o: Client-side validation only
Using HTTP rather than HTTPS for forms
Storing data in cookies
Parameterised queries on the server
q.why: Parameterised queries ensure input is never executed as SQL; client-side checks can be bypassed.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a web app over a native app?
o: One version works on any device with a browser
It always works fully offline
It has faster performance on the device
It has full access to the device's sensors
q.why: Web apps are cross-platform by nature; the other options are native-app advantages.

q.q: Why might a fitness tracker be built as a native app?
o: It needs offline use and full access to sensors such as GPS and Bluetooth
Native apps need no updates once they are installed on the device
Web apps cannot display numbers or charts in the browser
Native apps are found through search engines, so there are no store fees or approval rules
q.why: Sensors and offline running favour native apps.

q.q: How do users of a web app receive updates?
o: Each user downloads and installs them from the website
Through the platform's app store each week
Automatically, as soon as the server is updated
By being sent the new files by FTP
q.why: Everyone uses the server's current version, so old versions do not linger.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of native apps for the developer?
o: They cannot access the camera, GPS or Bluetooth on the device
A separate version must be built and maintained for each operating system
They can only run when there is a reliable internet connection
They cannot be found, bought or installed through any of the app stores
q.why: Native apps are written per OS, and stores charge fees and impose approval rules.

q.q: Why do native apps usually perform better than web apps?
o: They are downloaded fresh from the server each time they open
They store all their data on the publisher's server
They are written in HTML, which runs much faster on any device than JavaScript does
They are compiled for the device rather than running inside the browser
q.why: Running inside a browser adds overhead; native code is built for the device.

q.q: Which feature do progressive web apps (PWAs) add to narrow the gap with native apps?
o: They cache content for offline use and can be added to the home screen
They are compiled separately for each operating system's app store
They have full access to all sensors and run fully in the background
They must be downloaded and installed before they can be used
q.why: PWAs are still delivered from the web but gain some native-like features.

q.q: A Belfast arts centre wants people to buy tickets from any phone or laptop, including one-off visitors. Which is the best choice?
o: A native app, because offline use is essential for buying tickets
A web app, because there is no install barrier and seat data must be live anyway
A native app, because the camera and Bluetooth must be used to scan every ticket
A web app, because it will work with no signal on the hillside
q.why: Occasional users should not have to install anything, and booking needs a connection for live seat data.

q.q: Which is a drawback of publishing through an app store?
o: Users cannot discover the app through searching the store
Updates reach every user instantly
The store takes fees and imposes approval rules
The app cannot use the device's camera
q.why: Store listing aids discovery but brings fees and approval.

q.q: Which is a benefit of an e-service to the provider rather than the consumer?
o: Customers can compare prices and products easily
Customers can shop at any time of day or night
Customers save time and money by not travelling to the shop in person
Data about customers' preferences can give a competitive advantage
q.why: The other three benefit consumers.

q.q: What is e-government?
o: Governments regulating the companies that provide online shopping and banking
Governments monitoring citizens' and businesses' use of the Internet electronically to prevent crime
Governments delivering information and services to citizens and businesses electronically
Governments running elections entirely through electronic voting machines
q.why: It ranges from publishing information through transactions to participation.

q.q: Renewing vehicle tax online is an example of which level of e-government?
o: Publishing information
Participation
Portlets
Transactions
q.why: Transactions include renewing licences, filing tax returns and applying for benefits; petitions are participation.

q.q: Which disadvantage of e-government must be managed?
o: E-government is only available during office hours
People without internet access, skills or confidence could be excluded
E-government is slower and dearer than the paper processes that it replaces
E-government cannot accept any payments
q.why: Alternative channels such as phone, post and assisted digital help are still needed.

q.q: What is a portal?
o: A website or page giving consistent access to many related services from one starting point
A private network of web pages and services available only to an organisation's own signed-in staff
The point where an ISP connects its customers to its own network
A program that follows links to discover new pages for a search engine
q.why: Example: a council site linking bin collections, planning and rates in one place.

q.q: What is a portlet?
o: A small network port on a home router
A block of grouped links within a portal
A type of tracking cookie
A page listing apps on an app store
q.why: Portals organise their content into portlets, which users may be able to rearrange.

q.q: A school site lets pupils sign in once to reach timetables, homework, reports and payments. What is this?
o: A search engine
A public e-service
A native application
An enterprise portal
q.why: An enterprise portal links an organisation's own services, usually after a single sign-in.

q.q: What is an intranet?
o: A private network of web pages and services for an organisation's authorised members
The public Internet as accessed from inside an organisation's buildings
A company that connects an organisation's offices to the Internet
A search engine that indexes only the pages of one organisation's own public website
q.why: It uses web technologies but is closed to outsiders.

q.q: Why does an intranet help ensure staff use the latest version of a policy?
o: It emails every new version to all staff
It blocks access to the Internet while staff are reading the policy, so they cannot use old copies
Documents are edited in one place, so out-of-date copies are no longer available
It prints copies for every department automatically
q.why: Central publishing removes old copies.

q.q: Which measure best reduces the risk of a stolen password exposing intranet data?
o: Caching every page on a proxy server
Multi-factor authentication
A larger file server
Persistent cookies
q.why: With MFA a password alone is not enough to sign in.

q.q: Which law governs how an intranet must process staff personal data in the UK?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
PECR on its own
The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
q.why: Personal data held on an intranet must be processed lawfully under data protection law.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of an organisation relying on its intranet?
o: Confidential material is kept off the public Web
Content can be targeted to different groups of staff
If the intranet goes down, work is badly disrupted
Paper forms are replaced by online tools
q.why: Heavy dependence is a risk; the other options are advantages.

q.q: Why might an intranet need dedicated staff?
o: Content must be kept accurate and current
Intranets cannot be backed up automatically
Every page must be retyped each year
Staff cannot sign in without help
q.why: Clear content ownership keeps pages up to date.

q.q: Which measure reduces the risk that staff see confidential documents they do not need?
o: Role-based access rights
Regular backups
Redundant servers
A larger proxy cache
q.why: Role-based rights show each group only what it needs.

q.q: What makes an intranet evaluation for an 8-mark question strong?
o: Two separate lists of general advantages and disadvantages with no conclusion
A detailed description of how HTTP and HTML work inside the organisation
A list of every security measure that is available, without linking any of them to a particular risk
Points applied to the organisation, with a justified conclusion and a risk-reducing measure
q.why: Examiners reward balance, application to the scenario and a reasoned judgement.

q.q: What does encryption mainly provide?
o: Smaller files
Confidentiality
Proof of who sent a message
Faster transfer
q.why: Intercepted ciphertext is useless without the key. Proof of origin comes from digital signatures.

q.q: Ann wants to send Ben a confidential message using public key encryption. Which key does she use to encrypt it?
o: Ben's private key
Ann's private key
Ben's public key
Ann's public key
q.why: Encrypt with the recipient's public key so only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

q.q: A Belfast laboratory encrypts results with a GP practice's public key. Who can decrypt them?
o: Only the GP practice, using its own private key
Anyone who has the GP practice's public key
Only the laboratory, using its own private key
Anyone who intercepts the message and the public key
q.why: The public key cannot decrypt what it encrypted; only the matching private key can.

q.q: What is the main problem with symmetric encryption over the Internet?
o: It is too slow for large amounts of data
It cannot encrypt text, only images
It needs a digital certificate for every message
The secret key must be shared securely in advance
q.why: Key distribution between strangers is difficult; symmetric encryption is actually fast.

q.q: Which is true of public key encryption?
o: The same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data
Knowing the public key does not allow anyone to work out the private key
It is much faster than symmetric encryption, so it suits bulk data
The private key is published freely so that anyone can send messages
q.why: The keys are mathematically linked but the private key cannot be derived from the public one.

q.q: Why do secure connections use symmetric encryption for the bulk of the data?
o: It needs no key at all
It is required by DNS
It is much faster than public key encryption
It solves the key distribution problem between strangers
q.why: Public key methods are slow, so they are used only to agree the session key.

q.q: In a hybrid encryption system, what is public key encryption used for?
o: Encrypting every byte of the web page
Compressing the data before it is sent
Translating the domain name to an IP address
Agreeing a random symmetric session key securely
q.why: The session key then encrypts the data quickly; this is how TLS works.

q.q: Which row correctly compares symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
o: Symmetric: one shared key, fast; asymmetric: key pair, slow but easy key distribution
Symmetric: key pair, slow; asymmetric: one shared key, fast but hard to distribute
Symmetric: one shared key, slow; asymmetric: key pair, fast with easy distribution
Symmetric: key pair, fast; asymmetric: one shared key, slow and easy to distribute
q.why: Public keys can be published, which solves distribution, but the maths makes it slower.

q.q: Which is the correct order of the main TLS handshake steps?
o: Agree session key, exchange greetings, check certificate, encrypt data with the private key
Exchange greetings and certificate, check certificate, agree session key, encrypt data symmetrically
Check certificate, encrypt data symmetrically, exchange greetings, agree session key
Exchange greetings, encrypt data with the public key, check certificate, agree session key
q.why: The certificate is checked before a session key is agreed; all further data uses the symmetric session key.

q.q: What does a browser check about a site's digital certificate?
o: That it contains the site's private key and the owner's password
That the site has a high PageRank and many links to it
That it is signed by a trusted CA, in date, and issued for this domain
That the site is honest and its products are genuine
q.why: A certificate proves identity, not honesty.

q.q: Which item is never found in a digital certificate?
o: The owner's private key
The owner's public key
The validity dates
The issuing CA
q.why: The private key is always kept secret by its owner.

q.q: What does a digital certificate do?
o: Encrypts a document with the sender's private key to prove who sent it
Stores the shared session key used to encrypt data during a connection
Records which pages a user has visited so the site can remember them
Binds a public key to its verified owner, signed by a certificate authority
q.why: Do not confuse a certificate with a signature or a session key.

q.q: What does HTTPS NOT protect against?
o: Eavesdroppers reading data in transit
Undetected tampering with data in transit
A phishing site that has its own valid certificate
Connecting to an impostor server pretending to be the named domain
q.why: HTTPS proves you are connected to the domain in the certificate, not that the site is honest.

q.q: Which key is used to create a digital signature?
o: The sender's public key
The sender's private key
The recipient's public key
A shared symmetric key
q.why: Only the sender's private key can produce a signature that their public key verifies.

q.q: What is encrypted with the sender's private key to form a digital signature?
o: A hash of the document
The whole document
The recipient's public key
The CA's certificate
q.why: The sender hashes the document and encrypts the short hash value.

q.q: A receiver decrypts a signature with the sender's public key and hashes the document again, but the two values differ. What does this show?
o: The document is genuine and has not been changed in transit
The document has been altered or did not come from that sender
The receiver used the wrong private key to decrypt the message
The certificate authority has revoked the receiver's certificate
q.why: Matching hashes prove authenticity and integrity; a mismatch means tampering or a different signer.

q.q: What does a digital signature prove?
o: That the document is confidential
That the recipient has read the document
Who sent the document and that it has not been altered
That the sender's website and business are honest and genuine
q.why: Signatures give authenticity and integrity, not secrecy.

q.q: Which protections does TLS provide for data in transit?
o: Confidentiality, proof of honesty and protection from weak passwords
Compression, integrity and authentication of every user
Confidentiality only, with no check on the server's identity
Confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server
q.why: Data is encrypted, tampering is detected and the server is authenticated by its certificate.
